1.explanation: The PHP syntax-definition files in Highlight.js are responsible for recognizing PHP-specific tokens. "php.js" defines the main PHP grammar, and "php-template.js" handles PHP embedded in other files (e.g. HTML). Neither file currently includes a mode to match and style PHP variables (dollar-prefixed identifiers), so variables never receive the “variable” CSS class. To fix the bug, you’d add a regex mode for PHP variables in these files’ contains array, ensuring “$response” and similar tokens are highlighted correctly.
1.bug_scenario: When rendering PHP snippets with Highlight.js, PHP variables (for example, “$response”) aren’t being given the “variable” CSS class. In the screenshots we see the expected behavior—a green-highlighted variable—versus the actual behavior with no special styling on “$response”. This makes PHP code much harder to read.

2.explanation:
• src/languages/php.js is the main language definition for PHP in highlight.js. It is responsible for declaring the pattern that matches PHP variables (the “$foo” syntax). A missing or incorrect regex here would prevent variables from ever being tokenized as ‘variable’.  
• src/languages/php-template.js handles embedded PHP inside template files (HTML + PHP). It also needs a variable rule so that when PHP is interleaved with HTML, the PHP variables are recognized.  
• src/languages/lib/c-like.js provides common C-style grammar rules that many languages (including PHP) inherit from, such as punctuation, number, and variable patterns. If php.js relies on an inherited variable rule here, an issue in c-like.js could be affecting php.js’s variable highlighting.
2.bug_scenario: When highlighting PHP code snippets, variable names (e.g. $response) are not being picked up and styled as variables. In the expected rendering (first screenshot), PHP variables are highlighted in a distinct color. In the actual rendering (second screenshot), the variables are shown in the default text color, making the code hard to read.
